accept: decrease in velocity per unit time
rubric.why: Identifies retardation as the rate at which velocity decreases.
rubric.description: Defines retardation as a rate of decrease in velocity.
rubric.how: State that velocity decreases with time.

rubric.why: Shows the direction or sign of retardation.
rubric.description: Identifies retardation as acceleration opposite to the direction of motion, or as negative acceleration.
rubric.how: State that it acts opposite to velocity, or is negative acceleration.

modelAnswer: Retardation is the rate of decrease of velocity with time.
It is acceleration opposite to the direction of motion, so it is also called negative acceleration.

items.followUp: Why is friction necessary for walking?

rubric.why: Gives a consequence of losing the friction needed for walking.
rubric.description: States that walking would become impossible.
rubric.how: Explain that a person could not push against the ground to walk.

rubric.why: Gives another consequence of the disappearance of friction.
rubric.description: States that moving objects would not stop, vehicles could not stop, or objects could not be held securely.
rubric.how: Give one valid consequence of friction disappearing.

modelAnswer: Without friction, we could not walk because our feet would slip on the ground.
Moving objects would not stop, and vehicles could not be brought to rest.

items.followUp: Why is the outer edge of a road raised on a curved track?

rubric.why: Identifies which side of the road is raised.
rubric.description: States that the outer edge of the curved road is raised.
rubric.how: Name the outer edge or outer side.

rubric.why: Describes the raised road surface that forms the bank.
rubric.description: States that the outer edge is higher than the inner edge, making the road inclined to the horizontal.
rubric.how: Compare the heights of the two edges or describe the road's inclination.

modelAnswer: Banking of a road is the raising of its outer edge above its inner edge at a curve.
This makes the road surface inclined to the horizontal.

items.followUp: Differentiate between stable and unstable equilibrium.

accept: comes back to its original position
rubric.why: Gives the defining behaviour of stable equilibrium after a small displacement.
rubric.description: States that a body in stable equilibrium returns to its original position after a slight displacement.
rubric.how: Describe what happens to the body after it is displaced slightly.

rubric.why: Gives the defining behaviour of neutral equilibrium after a small displacement.
rubric.description: States that a body in neutral equilibrium remains in its new position after a slight displacement.
rubric.how: Contrast its behaviour with stable equilibrium.

modelAnswer: In stable equilibrium, a body returns to its original position after a slight displacement.
In neutral equilibrium, a body remains in its new position after a slight displacement.

items.followUp: Write down the first condition for equilibrium.

accept: sum of clockwise torques equals sum of anticlockwise torques
rubric.why: States the balance of moments required for rotational equilibrium.
rubric.description: States that the sum of clockwise torques equals the sum of anticlockwise torques.
rubric.how: Write the equality of clockwise and anticlockwise moments.

rubric.description: States that the resultant torque about any axis is zero.
rubric.how: State the net torque condition for equilibrium.

modelAnswer: The second condition for equilibrium is that the sum of clockwise torques equals the sum of anticlockwise torques about any axis.
Therefore, the net torque acting on the body is zero.

items.followUp: Name one device that uses wind energy and state what it does.

rubric.why: Identifies wind, or moving air, as the source of the energy.
rubric.description: States that wind energy is the energy of moving air.
rubric.how: Identify the source as moving air.

rubric.why: Shows a useful application or output of wind energy.
rubric.description: States that wind energy can perform useful work or generate electricity.
rubric.how: Give a valid use, such as operating a windmill or generating electricity.

modelAnswer: Wind energy is the energy possessed by moving air.
It can be used to perform useful work, for example to generate electricity.

items.followUp: State Pascal's law and name one device based on it.

rubric.why: Names an application of Pascal's law.
rubric.description: Names a device or machine that applies Pascal's law.
rubric.how: Give one example, such as a hydraulic press, lift, or brakes.

accept: pressure applied to an enclosed fluid
rubric.why: Shows the pressure-transmission principle underlying the applications.
rubric.description: States that pressure applied to an enclosed fluid is transmitted through it.
rubric.how: Describe the transmission of pressure in the enclosed fluid.

modelAnswer: Pascal's law is applied in hydraulic machines.
Examples include hydraulic presses, hydraulic lifts, and hydraulic brakes.

items.followUp: Define pressure and write its SI unit.

rubric.description: Defines stress as force per unit area.
rubric.how: Write the ratio of force to area.

rubric.why: Gives the SI unit of stress.
rubric.description: States the SI unit as the pascal (Pa), equivalent to newton per square metre.

modelAnswer: Stress is the force acting per unit area of a body.
Its SI unit is the pascal (Pa), which is equal to N/m².
